title: Workflow Rules and Process Builder as legacy/migration topics
objectives: State that Workflow Rules and Process Builder are no longer the preferred automation tools and that support/updates were scheduled to end 31 December 2025.
Use the Migrate to Flow tool in a sandbox, then test, activate the Flow, and deactivate the source rule or process.
Map field-update-only Workflow Rules to Fast Field Updates and Process Builder processes to Actions and Related Records.
Explain that migration is not one-to-one and that existing processes can still be activated, deactivated, and edited after end of support.
diagnostic_question: An org still has active Workflow Rules and Process Builder processes in 2026. What does end of support mean, what tool do you use first, and what do you deactivate only after the Flow is tested?
definition: Workflow Rules and Process Builder are legacy declarative automation. Salesforce Help says they are no longer preferred, to plan a switch to Flow Builder, and that support and updates were scheduled to end 31 December 2025. After that date you can still activate, deactivate, and edit existing processes; new automations belong in Flow. The Migrate to Flow tool converts eligible rules and processes. ([Planning Your Switch](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.flow_migrate_to_flow_best_practices.htm); [Flow variable considerations — Process Builder note](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.flow_considerations_feature_variable.htm))
why_it_matters: Interviewers ask whether you would still build new Process Builder, how Migrate to Flow works, and why you deactivate the source. ‘They stopped working on 1 January 2026’ is a common false statement.
sixty_second_explanation: Think of analog phone switchboards that still complete calls after the manufacturer ended service. Workflow Rules and Process Builder can still route, but Salesforce no longer services them after 31 December 2025. Migrate to Flow is the conversion kit. Field-update-only rules become Fast Field Updates—the digital handset. You cut the analog board only after the new PBX is tested. The switchboard program is metadata; the calls are data.
deeper_explanation: Planning Your Switch: Workflow Rules and Process Builder are no longer preferred. With their pending retirement, go with Flow Builder for extensibility, application lifecycle management, and faster performance. Migrate in a sandbox first. Identify and remove redundant processes. Prioritize simple same-object field updates and email alerts. Migration is not one-to-one. Replace time-dependent workflow with scheduled paths. ([Planning Your Switch](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.flow_migrate_to_flow_best_practices.htm))

Help still prints: support and updates for Process Builder are scheduled to end as of 31 December 2025; see Workflow Rules & Process Builder End of Support. After that date you can continue to activate, deactivate, and edit existing processes. For new automations, create Flows. Use Migrate to Flow to migrate. ([Variable considerations](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.flow_considerations_feature_variable.htm))

Trailhead: if a Workflow Rule contains only field updates on the triggering record, Migrate to Flow sets Fast Field Updates. Processes migrate with Actions and Related Records; you can change optimization after. The tool supports partial migration for most Process Builder actions except some invocables. ([Understand automation changes](https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/projects/migrate-workflows-and-processes-to-flows/understand-automation-changes))

After a good test, activate the Flow and deactivate the converted rule or process so both do not fire. The tool does not delete the source. Managed-package Workflow/Process Builder is the vendor’s job—Needs verification of what you can edit.
Do not treat end of support as ‘the automations stopped running.’ Help’s after-date sentence is activate/deactivate/edit existing, not a hard runtime kill switch.

mental_model.analogy: An analog phone switchboard after the manufacturer ended service: calls can still complete, but there are no spare parts. Migrate to Flow is the conversion kit to a digital PBX. Cut over only after a test ring.
useful_mapping: Workflow Rule / Process Builder → analog switchboard still completing calls
31 December 2025 → end of manufacturer support, not automatic silence
Fast Field Updates → field-update-only rules becoming before-save
Actions and Related Records → Process Builder-style related work
Deactivate source after test → unplug the analog board so two systems do not ring
Sandbox first → test ring in the lab
Rule/process metadata → switchboard program; records → the calls
where_it_breaks: Some rules cannot migrate cleanly; you rebuild in Flow Builder.
Managed packages are not your analog board to rewire.
End of support is not the same sentence as end of runtime.
Time-dependent workflow maps to scheduled paths, not a perfect clock clone.

interview_explanation.thirty_seconds: Workflow Rules and Process Builder are legacy. Support ended 31 December 2025, but existing ones can still be edited and can still run. I migrate in a sandbox with Migrate to Flow, test, activate the Flow, then deactivate the source. I do not build new Process Builder.
interview_explanation.two_minutes: I refuse the myth that everything died on 1 January 2026. Help says activate/deactivate/edit still work. I inventory, drop redundant processes, and migrate simple field-update rules to Fast Field Updates. Process Builder becomes Actions and Related Records. I apply AUTO-010 entry criteria instead of cloning every diamond. Managed packages are the vendor’s problem. Cutover is activate Flow, deactivate source, so two bells do not ring.

terminology.plain: The older if/then automation that could field-update, email, task, or outbound-message.
terminology.precise: Legacy tool. New work belongs in Flow. Field-update-only rules often migrate to Fast Field Updates.
terminology.example: Rule: Opportunity Stage = Closed Won → field update.
terminology.non_example: A record-triggered Flow you just built.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Process Builder: later legacy tool with criteria diamonds and more actions.
terminology.boundary: Outbound messages are an integration neighbor, not fully redesigned here.

terminology.plain: The later click-together automation Salesforce is ending support for.
terminology.precise: Help: support/updates scheduled to end 31 December 2025; still activate/deactivate/edit existing; new automations in Flow.
terminology.example: Process on Case that updates Account and posts to Chatter.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Flow Approval Process: current investment, not this legacy pair.
terminology.boundary: Marketing Cloud Connect had a separate PB retirement path—do not generalize that article to all orgs.

terminology.plain: Salesforce no longer supports or updates the tool after the published date.
terminology.precise: Scheduled 31 December 2025. Not the same sentence as ‘automations stop executing.’ After the date: activate, deactivate, edit existing.
terminology.example: A 2019 Workflow Rule still firing in 2026 with no Support bug-fix path.
terminology.non_example: A Flow Salesforce is actively documenting.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Retirement / disabled create-new: related but not identical; verify current Setup whether new PB can be created.
terminology.boundary: Needs verification of create-new disablement in the specific org.

terminology.plain: Setup tool that converts eligible Workflow Rules and processes into Flows.
terminology.precise: Quick Find Migrate to Flow. Select the process/rule, migrate, test, activate Flow, deactivate source.
terminology.example: Sandbox migrate of a field-update Workflow Rule to a before-save Flow.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Change set: moves metadata; it does not convert PB to Flow.

terminology.plain: before-save Flow optimization used when the migrated rule only updated the triggering record.
terminology.precise: Trailhead: field-update-only Workflow Rules get this optimization because those Flows run much faster.
terminology.example: Migrated Closed Won date stamp as before-save.
terminology.non_example: A Process that created Tasks remaining as Fast Field Updates.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Actions and Related Records: the Process Builder default after migrate.
terminology.boundary: You can change optimization after migrate if the result is wrong—verify in Builder.

terminology.plain: after-save-style optimization for migrated processes that do more than stamp the same record.
terminology.precise: Trailhead: processes migrate with this setting; you may switch to Fast Field Updates afterward if appropriate.
terminology.example: Migrated process that updates Account from Opportunity.
terminology.non_example: A same-record-only field update that should have been before-save.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Flow Approval Process: not a PB migration output.
terminology.boundary: Invocable actions may be partial migrations.

terminology.plain: Workflow that waited a number of days/hours then acted.
terminology.precise: Planning Your Switch: replace with scheduled paths on record-triggered Flows.
terminology.example: Email 7 days after Stage = Negotiation → scheduled path.
terminology.non_example: A pause in a screen Flow.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Process Builder scheduled actions: same migration idea, rebuild if the tool cannot map them.
terminology.boundary: Time-based workflow queue vs Flow scheduled path timing: verify current Help.

terminology.plain: Turning off the Workflow Rule or process after the Flow is active so both do not fire.
terminology.precise: Release note: test, activate the Flow, deactivate the process you converted. The tool does not delete the source.
terminology.example: Activate LAB_ClosedWon_Stamp Flow, then deactivate the old rule.
terminology.non_example: Deleting the rule before the Flow is tested.
terminology.boundary: Package version errors can mention migratedFrom if the rule is still active—Needs verification if you package.

hands_on_lab.environment: Developer sandbox that still shows Workflow Rules or Process Builder. If the org cannot create new ones, use existing unused lab automations only.
starting_state_checks: Migrate to Flow appears in Setup.
steps: Inventory one active Workflow Rule or process and write its actions.
Run Migrate to Flow in sandbox (or document why the item is ineligible).
Debug the new Flow against the same record event.
Activate the Flow, deactivate the source, and confirm a single set of side effects.
guided_completion: If both remain active, you will see doubles.
If the tool set the wrong optimization, change it in Flow Builder and retest.
hands_on_lab.independent_challenge: Find a time-dependent action and write how a scheduled path would replace it (do not invent hours).
evidence: Notes on Fast Field Updates versus Actions and Related Records.
stop_recovery_cleanup: You may reactivate the source in sandbox if the Flow is wrong; do not delete until rollback is unnecessary.
Do not perform this cutover in production as the lab.

decision_table.signal: Someone asks you to build a new Process Builder in 2026.
decision_table.choose: Refuse and build a Flow in Flow Builder.
decision_table.not: Create new Process Builder because the team ‘knows it’.
decision_table.why: Help: for new automations, create flows in Flow Builder.

decision_table.signal: A Workflow Rule only field-updates the triggering record.
decision_table.choose: Migrate to Flow and keep Fast Field Updates.
decision_table.not: Migrate then switch it to after-save Update Records without a reason.
decision_table.why: Trailhead: those rules get Fast Field Updates because they run much faster.

decision_table.signal: A Process Builder updates related records or creates Tasks.
decision_table.choose: Migrate as Actions and Related Records, then apply entry criteria and bulk-safe DML.
decision_table.not: Expect Fast Field Updates to Create related Tasks.
decision_table.why: Trailhead maps processes to Actions and Related Records; before-save cannot Create related rows.

decision_table.signal: The Migrate to Flow tool reports unsupported actions.
decision_table.choose: Rebuild those pieces in Flow Builder; treat the tool output as partial.
decision_table.not: Force-activate an incomplete Flow and delete the process.
decision_table.why: Trailhead: partial migration; some invocables need more work.

decision_table.signal: Sandbox Flow matches the legacy behavior.
decision_table.choose: Activate the Flow, deactivate the source rule or process, then watch one event.
decision_table.not: Leave both active in production ‘just in case’.
decision_table.why: Official sequence is test, activate Flow, deactivate the converted process.

limitations: Does not teach every Workflow action type in depth.
Eligibility matrices change; use the org’s tool, not memory.
End of support is not proven here as a runtime kill switch.
security_notes: Migrated Flows inherit data access issues; review AUTO-009 context.
Do not migrate in production as the first move.
Email alerts in legacy rules can contain PII; treat test records as LAB_.
common_mistakes: Saying the tools stopped running on 1 January 2026.
Leaving source and Flow both active.
One-to-one diamonds with no entry criteria.

check: A second Flow already doing the same job

troubleshooting.symptom: Migrate to Flow is disabled or empty.

troubleshooting.do_not_assume: You must keep Actions and Related Records.

production_notes: Cut over one object at a time during a quiet window.
Keep the source deactivated, not deleted, until the rollback window ends.
Re-run Explorer and a bulk test (AUTO-007) after migrate.

interview_questions.question: What is the status of Workflow Rules and Process Builder?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: They are legacy. Support and updates were scheduled to end 31 December 2025. You can still activate, deactivate, and edit existing ones. New automation is Flow.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I cite Planning Your Switch and the EOS note. I refuse ‘they all died on New Year’s Day.’ I explain Migrate to Flow, sandbox first, deactivate source. I mention Fast Field Updates versus Actions and Related Records. I do not build new Process Builder in 2026.
interview_questions.example: A 2018 Workflow Rule still active in 2026, unsupported, waiting to migrate.
tradeoffs: Migrate now vs accept unsupported runtime

interview_questions.question: How does Migrate to Flow work at a high level?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: In Setup, pick an eligible rule or process, convert it to a Flow in sandbox, test, activate the Flow, deactivate the source. Field-update-only rules become Fast Field Updates.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I inventory first and drop redundant processes. I use the tool when eligible and rebuild when it says partial or unsupported. I apply AUTO-010 so I do not clone every diamond. I set Explorer order. I keep the source for rollback until we are confident, but not active.
interview_questions.example: Sandbox migrate of LAB_ Closed Won field-update rule.

interview_questions.question: After go-live of a migrated Flow, Closed Won emails send twice. What do you check?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Whether the Workflow Rule or process is still active, and whether another Flow already sends the same email.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I open the legacy list and the new Flow. Doubles are the analog board still plugged in. I deactivate the source, retest one Opportunity, and check Explorer for a second Flow. I do not add a Decision to ‘skip if already emailed’ as the first fix.
interview_questions.example: Rule Inactive = false next to the new after-save Flow.
tradeoffs: One Flow vs two overlapping Flows
follow_ups: How long do you keep the inactive rule?
What if a package owns one?

interview_questions.question: A process creates Tasks and updates the Account. The tool migrates it. What do you still design?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Treat it as Actions and Related Records. Add entry criteria, bulk-safe Create/Update, fault paths, and Explorer order. Do not leave it as an unfiltered after-save clone.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I walk AUTO-007 through AUTO-010 on the output. I check whether same-record stamps should move to Fast Field Updates in a second Flow. I test a bulk update. I deactivate the process only after that. Partial invocable actions get a rebuild, not a hope.
interview_questions.example: Migrated Case process that updates Account—needs Get/Update collection design.
tradeoffs: Keep one migrated Flow vs split before/after
follow_ups: What if it used a formula with custom metadata?

interview_questions.question: How do you prioritize what to migrate first?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Planning Your Switch: sandbox, remove redundant, start with simple same-object field updates and email alerts, then harder related-record processes.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I pick the object with the fewest rules to learn the path. I migrate field-update-only rules to Fast Field Updates for a quick win. I do not start with the hairiest Process Builder that calls Apex. I schedule time-dependent work as its own slice. I keep a rollback window.
interview_questions.example: First: Closed Won date stamp rule. Later: multi-criteria Case process.
follow_ups: How do you find unused processes?
weak_answer_warnings: Migrate everything Friday night in production

interview_questions.question: Migrate to Flow will not convert a rule. What next?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Read the ineligibility reason. Rebuild in Flow Builder. Do not stay on unsupported Workflow because the tool shrugged.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I check operators, outbound messages, and managed-package ownership. I rebuild with the same business outcome and better entry criteria. I document gaps. I do not invent that every rule is eligible. Trailhead lists features that block eligibility—I re-open that list rather than reciting an unofficial one.
interview_questions.example: Rule uses an unsupported operator; you rebuild a before-save Flow.
tradeoffs: Apex vs Flow for the leftover action
weak_answer_warnings: The tool is mandatory for every rule

interview_questions.question: Metadata versus data in a migration?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Rules, processes, and Flows are metadata. The Opportunities they stamp are data. Migrating does not move historical field values; it changes which automation will fire next.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: Change sets or a pipeline move the new Flow. I do not Data Loader the Workflow Rule. I use LAB_ records to prove parity. Time-based queues may still hold pending workflow actions—I would verify current Help before I claim what happens to those rows at deactivate.
interview_questions.example: Deploy the new Flow; the Closed Won dates already on records stay put.
tradeoffs: Metadata deploy vs pending time-based work
Sandbox data vs production pending queues

interview_questions.question: A lead says ‘Process Builder is fine, Support will still take our cases.’ Answer as of 2026.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Help scheduled end of support for 31 December 2025. Existing processes may still run and can be edited, but I will not plan new PB or rely on bug fixes. I migrate.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I distinguish runtime from support. I show Planning Your Switch. I offer a sandbox pilot this sprint. I will not create new Process Builder to ‘go faster.’ I mention that staying on unsupported automation is a risk acceptance the business must sign, not a silent default.
